Illuminated
il-LOO-mi-nay-ted
v. (enlightened; given light)
Greek photizo, to give light, to enlighten, from phos, light. Latin illuminare, to light up. In the early church illumination became a standing term for the enlightening that accompanies conversion.

Biblical Definition

But call to remembrance the former days, in which, after ye were illuminated, ye endured a great fight of afflictions. The writer is steadying a congregation that is weakening, and his method is to send them back to their own beginning. After ye were illuminated dates the events he is about to recall: light came, and then the fight came. That order matters. Illumination in Scripture is not the reward of a long Christian life but the opening act of it — God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. The light is God's own giving, and it is given at the start. What followed, in their case, was not relief but a great fight of afflictions, and the writer describes it without euphemism: partly, whilst ye were made a gazingstock both by reproaches and afflictions; and partly, whilst ye became companions of them that were so used. They had been publicly shamed and had chosen to stand with others being publicly shamed. He recalls it to them because they had done it once, gladly, and were now in danger of drawing back. The Lord's own claim stands behind the whole figure: I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): enlightened; illustrated; made light; instructed; furnished with clear views.

expand to see more

ILLUMINATE, v.t. To enlighten; to throw light on; to supply with light.

ILLUMINATE, v.t. To enlighten, as the mind; to cause to understand; to illustrate.

ILLUMINATED, pp. Enlightened; rendered light or luminous; instructed.

ILLUMINATION, n. The act of illuminating; that infusion of light into the mind which is derived from the Holy Spirit.

ENLIGHTEN, v.t. To make clear to the mind; to enable to see or comprehend truth; to instruct.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 10:32 — "But call to remembrance the former days, in which, after ye were illuminated, ye endured a great fight of afflictions;"

Hebrews 10:33 — "Partly, whilst ye were made a gazingstock both by reproaches and afflictions; and partly, whilst ye became companions of them that were so used."

2 Corinthians 4:6 — "For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ."

John 8:12 — "Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life."

Modern Corruption

Illumination is claimed either as a higher experience above ordinary faith or as a natural insight the mind achieves; Scripture makes it God's own shining into the heart at the outset of the Christian life.

expand to see more

Every generation produces a version of the two-tier Christian: the ordinary believer and the illuminated one, who has had a further experience the rest have not. The gnostic systems of the second century made this their whole architecture, and the pattern has recurred in mysticisms, perfectionisms, and second-blessing schemes since. Hebrews 10:32 uses the word of the entire congregation, at the beginning, as a plain date-marker for their conversion. Paul describes the same event as God commanding light to shine out of darkness in the heart — a creative act, done once, given to all who are Christ's.

The rationalist error empties the word from the other side, making illumination the mind's own arrival at religious insight through study or reflection. That cannot account for the language Scripture uses. The natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness unto him, neither can he know them; the impediment is not a shortage of information. Illumination is the Spirit giving sight, which is why the Reformed tradition ties it to effectual calling and regeneration rather than to persuasion. It is also why the writer of Hebrews can use it as a fixed point in his readers' past — something that happened to them, which they can be called to remember.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek photizo (G5461), to enlighten; phos (G5457), light; athlesis (G119), a contest or fight; theatrizo (G2301), to make a spectacle of.

expand to see more

Greek photizo (G5461) — to give light, to enlighten; rendered illuminated here and enlightened elsewhere.

Greek phos (G5457) — light; the Lord's own title, the light of the world.

Greek athlesis (G119) — a contest, an athletic struggle; rendered fight of afflictions, its only occurrence.

Greek theatrizo (G2301) — to make a public spectacle; rendered made a gazingstock.

Greek lampo (G2989) — to shine; God hath shined in our hearts.

Usage

"“after ye were illuminated” — a date-marker, at the beginning."

"“ye endured a great fight of afflictions” — what followed the light."

"“hath shined in our hearts” — the same act, described by Paul."
